facts.statement: Harpacochampsa lived during the Early Miocene epoch.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Miocene

facts.statement: The genus Harpacochampsa was described by Megirian, Murray, and Willis in 1991.
facts.quote: authority: Megirian, Murray & Willis 1991

facts.statement: Harpacochampsa is a poorly known crocodilian found at the Bullock Creek fossil site in the Northern Territory of Australia.
facts.quote: Harpacochampsa is a poorly known Early Miocene crocodilian from the Bullock Creek lagerstätte of the Northern Territory, Australia.

facts.statement: The known specimen includes a partial skull with a long, slender snout similar to a false gharial, indicating it was a fish-eater.
facts.quote: The current specimen consists of a partial skull and fragments of a long, slender snout reminiscent of that of a false gharial, demonstrating that it was a piscivore in life.

facts.statement: The genus name Harpacochampsa combines Greek words meaning 'to seize' and 'crocodile,' referencing the specialized premaxillary teeth.
facts.quote: The genus name is a combination of the Greek words "harpaco" (to seize) and "champsos" (crocodile), a nod to the anatomy of the premaxillary teeth and their inferred function.

facts.statement: Harpacochampsa had roughly circular premaxillae containing five teeth on each side, separated from maxillary teeth by a notch likely for an enlarged lower jaw tooth.
facts.quote: The premaxillae are roughly circular in shape and contain five teeth on each side, separated from the following maxillary teeth by a notch that presumably receives an enlarged dentary tooth, as in many other crocodilians.

facts.statement: The only preserved functional premaxillary tooth in Harpacochampsa faced slightly outward instead of straight down.
facts.quote: Notably, the only functional premaxillary tooth (the fifth) preserved in Harpacochampsa faces slightly outward rather than straight down.

facts.statement: Harpacochampsa was pseudoheterodont, meaning its premaxillary teeth varied greatly in size while its maxillary teeth were more uniform.
facts.quote: The size of the alveoli indicates that the premaxillary teeth differed greatly in size, making the crocodile pseudoheterodont, whereas the maxillary teeth are more uniform.

facts.statement: Unlike other crocodylids where the fifth maxillary tooth is largest, the fourth premaxillary tooth was the largest in Harpacochampsa.
facts.quote: Unlike in other crocodylids, in which the fifth maxillary tooth is the largest, in Harpacochampsa it is the fourth premaxillary tooth.

facts.statement: Harpacochampsa likely primarily ate fish and turtles, but its stout build suggests it may have also hunted medium-sized mammals.
facts.quote: Accordingly, it is thought that Harpacochampsa primarily fed on fish and possibly turtles, however given its relatively stout build compared to modern gharials, it is possible that it may have also taken medium-sized mammals as prey.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Harpacochampsa belongs to the Mekosuchinae, is a basal crocodyloid, or is a type of gavialid.
facts.quote: It was originally tentatively placed within a group of Australian crocodilians now known as the Mekosuchinae, although this has been frequently disputed, with other authors instead suggesting it may have been a more basal crocodyloid or a type of gavialid.

facts.statement: The classification of Harpacochampsa within Mekosuchinae has been questioned by various authors, making its exact position controversial.
facts.quote: However the taxon's inclusion within Mekosuchinae has since then been questioned by various authors and its exact position has become controversial.

facts.statement: Ristevski et al. (2021) recovered Harpacochampsa as one of the basalmost crocodyloids, neither a mekosuchine nor a gavialoid.
facts.quote: Another publication that recovered Harpacochampsa as neither being a mekosuchine nor a gavialoid is Ristevski et al. (2021). This paper described Gunggamarandu from the Pliocene to Pleistocene of Queensland as the first undisputed tomistomine of Australia. Although this confirms the presence of tomistines in Australia, Harpacochampsa itself was not found to be part of the group and instead recovered as one of the basalmost crocodyloids.

facts.statement: Harpacochampsa is classified in the family Crocodylidae.
facts.quote: familia: Crocodylidae

facts.statement: The subfamily classification for Harpacochampsa is uncertain and listed as Mekosuchinae with question marks.
facts.quote: subfamilia: ¿Mekosuchinae?

facts.statement: Harpacochampsa is an extinct crocodilian genus from the Miocene found in the Cañada Bullock lagerstätte in the Northern Territory.
facts.quote: Harpacochampsa camfieldensis es un género extinto de crocodiliano del Mioceno hallado en el lagerstatte de la Cañada Bullock del Territorio del Norte.

facts.statement: The known specimen consists of a partial skull and fragments of a thin snout that resembles that of the false gharial.
facts.quote: El espécimen consiste de un cráneo parcial y fragmentos de un delgado hocico que recuerda al del falso gavial.

facts.statement: Harpacochampsa has been tentatively classified within Mekosuchinae, though some experts disagree because it might be the only known mekosuchine with a long, thin snout.
facts.quote: Se ha clasificado de manera tentativa dentro de Mekosuchinae, aunque algunos expertos no están de acuerdo con esto, dado que H. camfieldensis podrían ser el único mekosuquino conocido con un hocico largo y delgado.

facts.statement: Its elongated snout indicates that Harpacochampsa was a piscivore in life.
facts.quote: Su hocico alargado demuestra que en vida era un piscívoro.

facts.statement: Harpacochampsa belongs to the parent group Gavialoidea.
facts.quote: Parent group: Gavialoidea

facts.statement: Harpacochampsa is classified as a reptile.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: Harpacochampsa lived from the Langhian to the Serravallian stages, between 15.98 and 11.63 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Langhian to Serravallian (15.98 to 11.63 million years ago)

rejected.quote: The type description estimates that Harpacochampsa may have reached a length of up to 4 m based on the proportions of living crocodiles, possibly even as much as 5 m.
